blocks.md: The docs state that `plan()` cannot be used inside a CUDA graph or `torch.compile` (PyTorch's model compiler). With `use_cuda_graph=True` the wrapper uses caller-provided index buffers and the batch size must stay fixed for its lifetime, so engines capture one graph per batch-size bucket (a fixed menu of sizes, smaller batches padded up). For decode output that is bit-for-bit the same whatever else is in the batch, the docs point to `fixed_split_size` or `disable_split_kv`.

blocks.question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
blocks.explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

blocks.question: Why does FlashInfer's split-KV reduction avoid atomic adds, unlike some Stream-K implementations?
options: Atomics are not available on Hopper
Atomic accumulation order varies between runs, so outputs would not be deterministic
Atomics would use too much workspace
LSE values cannot be added
blocks.explain: The paper says LLM serving requires deterministic outputs, so it dropped Stream-K's atomic aggregation. The plan fixes a reduction map, and the contraction kernel merges partial states in the same order every time the same lengths appear.

lessons.title: Prefill and decode in one launch: POD and persistent batches

blocks.md: Picture one step of an engine that uses **chunked prefill** (a long prompt is processed a slice per step, so ongoing decodes are not stalled behind it): 64 requests each decode one token, and one new request contributes a 2,048-token prompt chunk. The linear layers process all 2,112 tokens together, so each weight is read once. Attention cannot be merged that way, because each request attends to its own KV. So the step usually runs two attention kernels: a prefill kernel for the chunk and a decode kernel for the 64 single tokens. vLLM's FlashInfer backend, for example, runs a decode kernel on the decode rows and a prefill kernel on the rest (the optional vLLM attention backends course, outside this course's prerequisites, shows how the batch is split).

Lesson 1's intensity formula says what goes wrong. The prefill chunk has thousands of query rows, so it is compute-bound: Tensor Cores are busy and HBM is mostly idle. The decodes have one query row each (4 with GQA), so they are memory-bound: HBM is busy and the Tensor Cores are mostly idle. Run them one after the other and each kernel wastes the resource the other one needs. The POD-Attention paper (Kamath et al., ASPLOS 2025, subtitled Unlocking Full Prefill-Decode Overlap) measured this for Llama 3 8B on A100s: the prefill attention kernel often used under 5% of memory bandwidth, and the decode kernel under 10% of compute.

How much could overlap save? A simplified roofline model (the Roofline course covers it in depth): each kernel takes the larger of its compute time (FLOPs over peak) and its memory time (bytes over bandwidth). Run back to back, the times add. Perfectly overlapped in one launch, the step takes the larger of total compute and total memory. The script uses one layer of Llama 3 8B (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, width 4096, so 4 KiB of K and V per token per layer), attention FLOPs of 4 x context x width per query token as in the GPU basics course, and the H100 figures from lesson 1.

blocks.code:
# Idealized roofline toy: one layer of Llama 3 8B attention on an H100, BF16
PEAK, BW = 989e12, 3.35e12             # FLOP/s and HBM bytes/s
W, KV, Q = 32 * 128, 2 * 8 * 128 * 2, 32 * 128 * 2  # width; K+V and Q bytes/token

def prefill(chunk, before):            # causal chunk after `before` cached tokens
    keys = chunk * before + chunk * (chunk + 1) // 2
    return 4 * keys * W, 2 * chunk * Q + (before + chunk) * KV

def decode(batch, ctx):
    return batch * 4 * ctx * W, batch * (ctx * KV + 2 * Q)

def us(f, b):                          # (compute time, memory time) in microseconds
    return f / PEAK * 1e6, b / BW * 1e6

for before, ctx in [(0, 1024), (8192, 4096), (0, 4096)]:
    (pc, pm), (dc, dm) = us(*prefill(2048, before)), us(*decode(64, ctx))
    seq = max(pc, pm) + max(dc, dm)    # two kernels, one after the other
    fused = max(pc + dc, pm + dm)      # perfect overlap in one launch
    print(f"chunk@{before} + 64 x {ctx}: prefill {pc:.1f}/{pm:.1f} us, "
          f"decode {dc:.1f}/{dm:.1f} us, {seq:.1f} vs {fused:.1f} us, {seq/fused:.2f}x")
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU. Real output, compute/memory times per kernel: chunk at 0 with 64 decodes of 1024 tokens gives 115.2 vs 93.0 us (1.24x); chunk at 8192 with decodes of 4096 gives 633.5 vs 343.4 us (1.85x); chunk at 0 with decodes of 4096 gives 355.6 vs 333.4 us (1.07x). Idealized peaks, not measurements.

blocks.title: One layer: prefill chunk at 8192 plus 64 decodes of 4096 (model)

scenes.caption: Two kernels in sequence. The prefill chunk needs 312.7 us of math but only 22.5 us of memory traffic; then the decodes need 320.8 us of memory but 4.3 us of math. The step ends at 633.5 us.
One fused launch with perfect overlap: decode KV streams from HBM while prefill tiles keep the Tensor Cores busy. The step takes the larger total, 343.4 us of memory: 1.85x faster in this model.
A step with only the 64 decodes: nothing compute-bound to hide, so one launch or two makes no difference. Both take 320.8 us of KV reads.

blocks.title: Ideal speedup of one fused launch over two kernels (model)

scenes.caption: The gain is largest when the prefill's compute time and the decodes' memory time are similar (1.85x), and small when one side dwarfs the other (1.07x). With no prefill in the batch there is nothing to overlap.

blocks.md: Getting near that ideal is harder than launching both kernels at once. The paper tested the obvious routes in its Section 3. Two CUDA streams, or one kernel whose thread blocks are split between the two jobs, do not guarantee that a prefill CTA and a decode CTA ever share an SM; in its microbenchmark they gained 7% and 3% on average. Splitting warps inside each CTA between the jobs does co-locate them, but a CTA cannot be replaced until its slowest warp finishes (stragglers). Interleaving the two jobs inside each thread did better (13%), but the barriers attention kernels use to coordinate shared-memory loads limit it.

POD's answer is **SM-aware CTA scheduling** inside one kernel. When the hardware places a CTA on an SM, its first thread reads the SM's ID from a hardware register (`%smid`), takes a ticket from that SM's counter with an atomic add, and only then decides whether this CTA does prefill or decode work. A policy maps tickets to jobs: alternate 50:50, or proportional to the batch's ratio of prefill and decode CTAs. If one job's CTAs are all handed out, the CTA switches to the other. Supporting choices from the paper:

- Decode uses a 16-row query tile, the minimum CUTLASS needs for A100 Tensor Core operations, so padded decode rows do not steal Tensor Core time from the co-running prefill.
- 2 CTAs per SM for prefill-heavy batches, 4 otherwise, chosen at run time.
- Each decode CTA is split into one-warp virtual CTAs so both jobs need similar shared memory.
- Prefill KV splits are capped at two waves of CTAs, so they do not flood HBM.

blocks.title: SM-aware scheduling: each CTA picks its job after it lands

scenes.caption: A batch needs 4 prefill CTAs and 4 decode CTAs; each SM holds 4 CTAs. The hardware places CTAs wherever it likes. Simplified: two SMs, 50:50 policy.
A CTA lands on SM 0, reads its SM ID, gets ticket 0 from SM 0's counter and becomes a prefill CTA. The next one on SM 0 gets ticket 1: decode.
Whatever order CTAs arrive in, tickets alternate per SM, so every SM ends up running both kinds: Tensor Cores and memory stay busy on each one.
Without the ticket step, the hardware could fill SM 0 with prefill CTAs and SM 1 with decode CTAs: the same kernel, but each SM idles one resource again.

blocks.md: Results reported in the paper, on A100s: attention up to 59% faster (28% on average) than separately optimized FlashAttention and FlashInfer prefill and decode kernels, over a thousand hybrid batches; and, integrated into the Sarathi-Serve scheduler, up to 22% higher end-to-end throughput. Gains peaked when most batches were hybrid, and shrank when many steps were decode-only or prefill-only. The paper also measured the shortcut of running decodes through the prefill kernel: with a prefill-sized tile, the padded decode rows waste compute, and that was up to 40% slower at long contexts.

In FlashInfer, POD appears as two wrappers in `flashinfer.pod`. `PODWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` runs a single-request prefill and a batch decode in one launch: `plan()` takes the decode page table, and `run()` takes the prefill's `q_p`, `k_p`, `v_p` and the decode queries `q_d` with the paged cache, returning `(out_p, out_d)`. `BatchPODWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` plans both halves from their own `qo_indptr`, `kv_indptr`, `kv_indices` and `kv_last_page_len`, as below. On the scheduler side, the prefill planner subtracts the CTAs that will be co-located with decode work from its 2-per-SM budget (`num_colocated_ctas` in scheduler.cuh).

blocks.code:
# Abridged from the BatchPODWithPagedKVCacheWrapper example in the docs. GPU only, not run here.
wrapper = flashinfer.BatchPODWithPagedKVCacheWrapper(workspace, "NHD")
wrapper.plan(
    p_qo_indptr, p_kv_indptr, p_kv_indices, p_last_page_len,   # 2 prefills of 2048
    d_qo_indptr, d_kv_indptr, d_kv_indices, d_last_page_len,   # 128 decodes of 2048
    num_qo_heads=64, num_kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, page_size=1,
    q_data_type=torch.bfloat16, kv_data_type=torch.bfloat16)
for layer in range(num_layers):           # one plan serves every layer
    o_p, o_d = wrapper.run(q_p, kv_p, q_d, kv_d, causal_p=True)
# o_p: [4096, 64, 128]   o_d: [128, 64, 128]
blocks.caption: Output shapes are from the docs example. Like every wrapper, plan() runs once per step on the CPU and run() once per layer.

blocks.md: A second route to one launch is **persistent batch attention**: `flashinfer.BatchAttention`, which the docs call a holistic wrapper that fuses paged prefill and paged decode requests into a single kernel launch. Its plan (`TwoStageHolisticPlan` in scheduler.cuh) puts each request in one of two task lists. If its fused query length, query tokens times the GQA group size, is above 16, it goes to a prefill-style list with 128-row query tiles; otherwise to a decode-style list with 16-row tiles. Then lesson 4's machinery runs: KV is cut into chunks (the limit is rounded up to a multiple of 256, and cut by up to half for the prefill-style list because those tiles cost more), and a min-heap hands the work to a fixed grid of 2 persistent CTAs per SM (1 for head dimension 256 or more).

The overlap numbers above are an upper bound from a peak-rate model. Fused CTAs still compete with each other: for Tensor Cores (why POD shrinks decode tiles), HBM bandwidth (why it caps prefill splits) and shared memory (why it splits decode CTAs into one-warp virtual CTAs). And a misconception to drop: "one kernel for the whole batch" is not enough by itself. Pushing decodes through a prefill kernel is one launch too, and the paper found it up to 40% slower at long contexts.

blocks.prompt: An engine serves a chat workload where new prompts are rare: 95% of steps are decode-only. Should it expect POD to speed up attention in those steps?
blocks.reveal: No. A decode-only step has no compute-bound work to overlap, so one launch or two costs the same: the decode kernel is limited by KV reads either way (the last timeline scene). POD only helps hybrid steps, which is why the paper's end-to-end gains peaked for workloads where most batches mixed prefill and decode, and shrank when decode-only steps dominated.

blocks.question: In which batch does fusing prefill and decode attention into one launch help MOST, by the roofline model?
options: 64 decodes of 4K tokens and no prefill
One 8K-token prefill chunk at position 32K and 64 decodes of 1K tokens
A prefill chunk needing about 300 us of math alongside decodes needing about 300 us of KV reads
Any batch, because one launch always halves the time
blocks.explain: Overlap saves at most the smaller of the two kernels' bottleneck times, so it pays most when they are similar: about 1.85x in the lesson's model. A decode-only batch has nothing to hide. A huge prefill dwarfs the decodes (5.0 ms of math against 0.08 ms of reads), so the gain is about 2%. One launch can never beat the larger total of compute or memory.

blocks.question: Why does POD give decodes a 16-row query tile instead of FlashAttention's usual 64 or 128 rows?
options: A 16-row tile reads less KV from HBM
Larger tiles give wrong results for single-token queries
Decode CTAs need more shared memory than prefill CTAs
Padded decode rows would burn Tensor Core time that the co-running prefill needs
blocks.explain: A decode has 1 query row per KV head (a few with GQA), so a 128-row tile is mostly zero padding. Alone, a memory-bound decode kernel barely notices. Fused with a prefill on the same SM, that padded math competes for the Tensor Cores; the paper cut decode compute use to about 10% with 16-row tiles. Results are correct either way, and KV bytes read are the same.

blocks.md: Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound, so a hybrid step run as two kernels idles one resource at a time. POD fuses them in one launch and makes every SM run both kinds of CTA; FlashInfer ships it as POD wrappers, and BatchAttention reaches one launch with a persistent, load-balanced work list.

lessons.title: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants

blocks.md: FlashInfer's kernels come from CUDA/CUTLASS templates (CUTLASS is NVIDIA's open-source C++ template library for matrix-multiply kernels): the FlashAttention-2 algorithm for GPUs up to Ada (sm89, CUDA's name for compute capability 8.9, the generation of the L4 and L40) and FlashAttention-3 on Hopper, per the paper. A classic FlashAttention-2 (FA2) kernel uses one tile shape such as $(128, 64)$ (query rows by KV columns), ideal for prefill but wasteful for decode, where a request has 1 query row.

So FlashInfer compiles FA2 kernels for query tiles $\{1, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$ times KV tiles $\{32, 64, 128\}$ and picks one per batch: the smallest query tile at least as large as the average (fused) query length, then a KV tile sized for occupancy (how many thread blocks fit on an SM at once, which lets the SM hide memory waits) under register and shared-memory limits. A worked instance of the shipping rule follows the quiz below. Query tile 1 uses CUDA cores (the ordinary scalar arithmetic units) because a Tensor Core MMA (matrix multiply-accumulate) instruction needs at least 16 rows; FA3 tiles are multiples of 64 to fit Hopper's warpgroup matrix multiply-accumulate instruction, which a group of 4 warps issues together and whose tile is 64 rows tall.

What is a "fused" query length? Appendix A describes **head-group fusion** for GQA. Instead of one thread block per query head, FlashInfer maps one KV head to a thread block and stacks that group's query heads into the row dimension. A decode step with group size $g = 8$ therefore looks like a query of 8 rows against one KV stream: each KV tile is loaded into shared memory once and used by all 8 heads. A request has several query tokens in one step during chunked prefill, or in speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes a few tokens and the large model checks them all in one pass.

blocks.title: Head-group fusion: one KV head, its 4 query heads, 2 query tokens

scenes.caption: GQA with $g = 4$ query heads per KV head and 2 new query tokens (for example a speculative-decoding step). Simplified: the exact row order is an implementation detail.
Fused, this is one block of $2 \cdot 4 = 8$ query rows that all read the same KV head. The tile rule picks query tile 16, the smallest one of at least 8, which can run on Tensor Cores.
Without fusion each head would be a separate 2-row problem: query tile 16 would be 7/8 empty, and the KV head would be loaded 4 times.

blocks.question: A batch has average query length 3 per request and GQA group size 8. Which query tile size does FlashInfer's heuristic choose?
options: 32, the smallest tile of at least 3 x 8 = 24 rows
1, because it is mostly decode
16, the smallest Tensor Core tile
128, the prefill default
blocks.explain: With head-group fusion the effective query length is $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ rows. The rule takes the smallest tile meeting or exceeding it among 1, 16, 32, 64, 128, which is 32. Choosing 16 would need two tiles; 128 would waste most of the rows.

blocks.md:
**One KV tile choice, computed.** The FA2 prefill dispatch in FlashInfer's source (`prefill.cuh` at commit `e2d163f`) picks the KV tile from shared memory and a register rule. Take head dimension 128 in FP16, query tile 64, on an A100 (164 KB of shared memory per SM, 163 KB per block, from the CUDA guide). That kernel runs 4 warps along the query rows, so each warp owns one 16-row query fragment.

1. Fixed cost: the Q tile, $64 \cdot 128 \cdot 2$ B = 16 KiB.
2. Each 16-row step of KV tile adds K and V rows: $16 \cdot (128 + 128) \cdot 2$ B = 8 KiB.
3. If two CTAs with the smallest tile fit on one SM ($2 \cdot 24$ KiB, yes), aim for 2 CTAs per SM, so each gets half: 83,968 B.
4. Steps that fit: $(83968 - 16384)/8192 = 8.25$, so 8.
5. Register cap: 8 steps divided by query fragments per warp (1), which keeps the score accumulator at $1 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 = 64$ FP32 registers per thread; the output accumulator takes another 64.
6. Take the smaller cap, round down to 8, 4, 2 or 1: 8 steps, a KV tile of 128 rows, 80 KiB per CTA.

blocks.code:
# FA2 KV-tile rule from FlashInfer's prefill.cuh, head_dim 128, FP16, A100
SM, OPTIN, D, B = 164 * 1024, 163 * 1024, 128, 2   # smem per SM, per block

def pick(cta_q):
    warps_q = 4 if cta_q > 16 else 1               # warps along query rows
    warps_kv = 4 // warps_q                        # warps along KV rows
    mma_q = 2 if cta_q > 64 else 1                 # 16-row Q fragments per warp
    fixed = cta_q * D * B                          # Q tile in shared memory
    step = (D + D) * 16 * warps_kv * B             # K and V for 16 more KV rows
    ctas = 2 if SM >= 2 * (fixed + step) else 1    # aim for 2 CTAs per SM
    budget = min(SM // ctas, OPTIN)
    n = min((budget - fixed) // step, 8 // mma_q)  # smem cap, register cap
    n = max(x for x in (8, 4, 2, 1) if x <= n)
    return ctas, budget, n * warps_kv * 16, fixed + n * step

for cta_q in (16, 64, 128):
    ctas, budget, kv, smem = pick(cta_q)
    print(f"q tile {cta_q}: {ctas} CTAs/SM, budget {budget} B, KV tile {kv}, smem {smem} B")
for kv in (32, 64, 128):                           # q tile 64, by smem alone
    smem = 64 * D * B + kv * (D + D) * B
    print(f"KV tile {kv}: {smem} B per CTA, {SM // smem} CTAs fit per SM")
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU. Real output: q tile 16 gives KV tile 128; q tile 64 gives KV tile 128 at 81,920 B; q tile 128 gives KV tile 64 (2 query fragments per warp halve the register cap); KV tiles 32, 64, 128 at q tile 64 need 32,768, 49,152 and 81,920 B, so 5, 3 and 2 CTAs fit per SM by shared memory alone.

blocks.title: Query tile 64, head dim 128, FP16 on an A100

scenes.caption: By shared memory alone: 32 KiB, 48 KiB and 80 KiB per CTA, so 5, 3 or 2 CTAs fit in the SM's 164 KB. Smaller tiles allow more resident CTAs.

The rule does not chase the largest CTA count. It fixes 2 CTAs per SM, then spends that budget on the largest KV tile that fits: 128 rows. Each CTA then walks the KV sequence in a quarter as many steps as with tile 32.

blocks.md:
The second customization axis is the attention **variant**. It is inspired by FlexAttention, a PyTorch API where you write the score change as a small Python function and the compiler generates a fused attention kernel in Triton (OpenAI's Python-based language for GPU kernels). A FlashInfer variant is a small class of CUDA functors (C++ objects that are called like functions) that the JIT compiler pastes into the kernel template:

- `QueryTransform`, `KeyTransform`, `ValueTransform`: applied to Q, K, V before attention (fuse RoPE, normalization or a projection).
- `LogitsTransform` and `LogitsMask`: modify or mask scores before softmax (soft-cap; ALiBi, attention with linear biases, which adds to each score a penalty proportional to the query and key distance with a fixed slope per head; sliding window; custom masks). Soft-capping replaces each score $x$ with $c \tanh(x/c)$ for a cap $c$.
- `OutputTransform`: applied to the output.
- A `use_softmax` flag, so even non-softmax attention such as FlashSigmoid (which applies a sigmoid to each score instead of a softmax over the row) fits.

The paper summarizes the design space as $f_{epilogue}(\mathrm{scan}(f_{logits}(f_q(Q)\, f_k(K)))\, f_v(V))$. Read it from the inside out: transform Q and K and multiply them into scores, apply the logits transform, run scan over each row of scores (softmax by default), multiply by the transformed values, and finish with the epilogue, which is the output transform.

blocks.title: A logits soft-cap variant inside the kernel (sketch)

scenes.caption: The variant is a C++ class given to the JIT compiler as a code string, in the style of the paper's Figure 5. Extra parameters such as cap become kernel arguments.
The constructor runs once per thread block and copies parameters into registers.
The generated kernel calls LogitsTransform on every score in its register tile. A score of 10 becomes $30\tanh(1/3) = 9.645$: small scores barely change.
A score of 50 becomes 27.933 and 100 becomes 29.924: large scores are squashed below 30, so one key cannot dominate. Then the usual online softmax runs.

blocks.caption: The soft-cap formula from the FlashInfer decode docs (used by Gemma-2 and Grok). tanh is close to its input near 0 and flattens out at 1, so small scores pass almost unchanged and no score can exceed $c$ in size. Also built in as plan()'s logits_soft_cap.

blocks.md: Fusion is where variants pay off. The paper's StreamingLLM case study shows it. StreamingLLM lets a model generate past its trained length by keeping the first 4 tokens (attention sinks) plus a window of recent tokens; it caches keys before rotation and applies RoPE to them at their positions within the cache at every decoding step. FlashInfer fused RoPE into attention with about 20 extra lines of query/key transform, cutting end-to-end inter-token latency by 28 to 30% and reaching 1.6 to 3.7x higher bandwidth utilization than separate RoPE plus attention kernels. On H100 it also reports higher TFLOPs/s than FlexAttention for causal, soft-cap and ALiBi variants, which it credits to warp specialization (some warps only load data while others only compute), TMA and register-level control that Triton did not fully expose.

JIT has a cost: kernels compile on first use and are cached. The 0.2 release reports all kernels for Llama models JIT-compile in about 15 seconds on server CPUs, and the README offers optional `flashinfer-cubin` (a cubin is a compiled CUDA binary) and `flashinfer-jit-cache` packages with prebuilt kernels. Kernels are also generated per data type: Appendix F describes FP8 KV-cache kernels that keep queries and outputs in FP16 and convert KV on the fly; in the API you pass `kv_data_type` to plan() and optional `k_scale` and `v_scale` to run().

Where it stands and what it does not do:

- In SGLang on H100 the paper reports 29 to 69% lower inter-token latency than SGLang's Triton backend.
- In vLLM, FP8 KV cache gained about 13% ITL, but BF16 saw small regressions from host-side Python overhead in the integration (Appendix G.4).
- The paper's kernels are forward-only; training would need customizable backward templates.
- Wrappers take a `backend` argument when constructed. The default `"auto"` picks by GPU, features and batch shape: in the current source the paged prefill wrapper takes FA3 on Hopper when the variant and head dims are supported (FA2 when no request has more than 64 query tokens) and FA2 otherwise, and on newer GPUs it can resolve to further implementations from the docs (for example kernels from cuDNN, NVIDIA's deep neural network library, and from TensorRT-LLM, NVIDIA's LLM inference library). To pin one, name it, as in the code below.

blocks.code:
# Pin the FA2 template instead of letting "auto" choose (GPU only, not run here)
prefill = flashinfer.BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper(
    workspace, "NHD", backend="fa2")
prefill.plan(qo_indptr, kv_page_indptr, kv_page_indices, kv_last_page_len,
             num_qo_heads, num_kv_heads, head_dim, page_size, causal=True)
blocks.caption: Pinning helps when you compare backends or need identical numerics across GPU generations. backend is a constructor argument, not a plan() argument.

blocks.md: The paper's design in one line: one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged exactly so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

blocks.question: You want attention with RoPE applied inside the kernel (instead of a separate RoPE pass that writes rotated Q and K to HBM). Which variant hooks do you implement?
options: LogitsMask
OutputTransform
QueryTransform and KeyTransform
ValueTransform only
blocks.explain: RoPE rotates query and key vectors before their dot product, which is exactly what the query and key transform functors are for. The paper uses them for fused RoPE in StreamingLLM. A mask or output hook acts too late, and values are not rotated.

blocks.question: Why does FlashInfer pick a different query tile for decode than for long prefill instead of always using a large one?
options: Large tiles give wrong results for decode
A decode query has few rows, so a 128-row tile would be mostly padding and waste compute and shared memory
Small tiles have higher arithmetic intensity
Tile size must equal the page size
blocks.explain: Tile size affects efficiency, not correctness. With 1 to a few fused rows per request, a 128-row tile spends almost all of its work on empty rows. The paper notes the usual FA2 tile is good for prefill on A100 but inefficient for decode. Page size is independent of the query tile.

lessons.title: MLA in FlashInfer: attention over a compressed latent cache

blocks.md: Take one decode token in one layer of DeepSeek-V2 (DeepSeek-V3 keeps the same attention shape). It has 128 query heads, yet the cache row it reads for each past token is just 576 numbers, shared by every head. That is **multi-head latent attention (MLA)**, introduced in DeepSeek-V2. In one sentence (the optional Multi-head latent attention course, outside this course's prerequisites, derives it): each token stores a 512-wide compressed latent $c$ plus a 64-wide rotary key part $k^R$, and at decode time each head's key up-projection is folded into its query (**absorption**), so the heads score directly against the latent instead of rebuilding per-head keys.

blocks.tex: s_{t,j,i} = \big[\,W^{UK\top}_i q^C_{t,i}\,;\; q^R_{t,i}\,\big] \cdot \big[\,c_j\,;\; k^R_j\,\big], \qquad o_{t,i} = W^{UV}_i \sum_j a_{t,j,i}\, c_j
blocks.caption: Query token $t$, head $i$, past token $j$: $q^C$ is the 128-wide content query, $q^R$ the 64-wide rotary query, and $W^{UK}_i$, $W^{UV}_i$ the head's key and value up-projections. The score is a 576-wide dot product; the output mixes 512-wide latents with softmax weights $a$, then up-projects once.

blocks.md: Look at it as a kernel would. All 128 query heads read the **same** rows $[c_j; k^R_j]$: that is multi-query attention (one KV head) with a 576-wide key and a 512-wide value, and the value is simply the first 512 columns of the key row. In lesson 6's terms this is head-group fusion with $g = 128$: a single decode token already supplies 128 query rows that share every KV tile, enough to fill Tensor Core tiles. And by lesson 1's formula, intensity grows with $g$, so MLA decode sits far above ordinary GQA decode.

blocks.code:
# Decode attention, one layer, BF16 (2 bytes per element)
mla = (512 + 64) * 2            # MLA row: latent + RoPE key, shared by all heads
gqa = 2 * 8 * 128 * 2           # Llama 3 8B: K and V, 8 KV heads of dim 128
mha = 2 * 128 * 128 * 2         # 128 heads of dim 128 stored as plain MHA
print("bytes per token per layer:", mha, gqa, mla)

def intensity(rows, k_elems, v_elems, bytes_read):
    # FLOPs per cached token / bytes read for it (2 FLOPs per multiply-add)
    return 2 * rows * (k_elems + v_elems) / bytes_read

print("MHA", intensity(1, 128, 128, 2 * 128 * 2))           # 1 query row per KV head
print("GQA g=4", intensity(4, 128, 128, 2 * 128 * 2))
for s_q in (1, 2):                                          # query tokens per request
    print(f"MLA s_q={s_q}", round(intensity(128 * s_q, 576, 512, mla), 1))
print("H100 ridge", round(989e12 / 3.35e12, 1))
print("64 requests x 4096 tokens, MiB per layer:", 64 * 4096 * mla / 2**20, 64 * 4096 * gqa / 2**20)
blocks.caption: Runs on CPU. Real output: 65536, 4096 and 1152 bytes per token per layer; intensity 1.0 for MHA, 4.0 for GQA with g = 4, 241.8 and 483.6 for MLA with 1 and 2 query tokens per request; H100 ridge 295.2; 288.0 vs 1024.0 MiB per layer for 64 requests of 4,096 tokens.

blocks.title: KV cache bytes per token per layer (BF16)

scenes.caption: Storing 128 heads' keys and values as plain MHA would take 65,536 bytes per token per layer. Llama 3 8B's GQA with 8 KV heads takes 4,096 (the 128 KiB per token over 32 layers used across these courses).

MLA stores one 576-wide row: 1,152 bytes, 57x less than the MHA shape and 3.6x less than Llama 3 8B's GQA, even though it serves 128 query heads. 64 requests of 4,096 tokens read 288 MiB per layer instead of 1 GiB.

blocks.caption: FLOPs per cached token over bytes read for it, in BF16: every one of the $h_q s_q$ query rows does a 576-wide score and a 512-wide mix (2 FLOPs per multiply-add), while the 576-element row is read once. Same count as the MLA course (it uses FlashMLA's H800 ridge of 258, not the H100's 295).

blocks.title: Decode attention intensity, FLOPs per byte (BF16)

scenes.caption: Plain MHA decode does about 1 FLOP per byte and GQA with $g = 4$ about 4: both far below the H100 ridge of 295, deep in memory-bound territory (lesson 1).

MLA decode with 128 heads reaches 242 FLOPs per byte, close to the ridge. With 2 query tokens per request, as in speculative decoding or multi-token prediction (MTP), it reaches 484 and becomes compute-bound.

blocks.title: The absorbed MLA decode path inside one kernel

scenes.caption: Before attention, each head's query is multiplied by its absorbed key projection, giving q_nope (512 wide; nope means no positional encoding), while the rotated 64-wide part q_pe passes through as is. This happens outside the attention kernel.
The kernel scores all 128 heads against the shared ckv and kpe pages. Each page tile is loaded into shared memory once and used by every head.

Softmax weights then mix the same ckv rows again, now as values: K and V are the same data. The 512-wide result per head leaves the kernel, and the up-projection to the model width happens afterwards.

blocks.md: **Page layout.** FlashInfer's KV-layout tutorial stores the MLA cache as one paged tensor of shape `(max_num_pages, page_size, 512 + 64)` and slices it into `ckv` (compressed key/value, the first 512 columns) and `kpe` (key with positional encoding, the last 64) without copying. There is no head dimension, so the NHD versus HND choice from lesson 2 disappears. The page table itself is unchanged: `kv_indptr` and `kv_indices` exactly as before.

**The wrapper.** `flashinfer.mla.BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper` is meant for decode and incremental prefill with the absorbed form, per its docs; a long prompt's prefill uses the non-absorbed form through the regular prefill wrapper, because absorption trades fewer bytes for more FLOPs (the MLA course computes the crossover). Its `plan()` takes the page table in CSR form with one change: per-request lengths `kv_len` in tokens instead of `kv_last_page_len` (they carry the same information: last page length is $(\text{len} - 1) \bmod \text{page\_size} + 1$). It also takes `num_heads`, `head_dim_ckv=512`, `head_dim_kpe=64`, `page_size`, `causal` and `sm_scale`. `run()` takes `query=(q_nope, q_pe)` and `kv_cache=(ckv, kpe)`.

blocks.code:
# Following FlashInfer's MLA test (tests/attention/test_deepseek_mla.py). GPU only, not run here.
sm_scale = 1.0 / ((128 + 64) ** 0.5)   # head dim BEFORE absorption, not 576
wrapper = flashinfer.mla.BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper(workspace, backend="auto")
wrapper.plan(
    metadata=flashinfer.mla.MLAPlanMetadata.csr(q_indptr, kv_indptr, kv_indices, kv_lens),
    num_heads=128, head_dim_ckv=512, head_dim_kpe=64, page_size=64,
    causal=False, sm_scale=sm_scale,
    q_data_type=torch.bfloat16, kv_data_type=torch.bfloat16,
    query_layout="split", kv_cache_layout="split", lse_mode="base2")
o, lse = wrapper.run(query=(q_nope, q_pe), kv_cache=(ckv, kpe), return_lse=True)
# q_nope: [tokens, 128, 512]  q_pe: [tokens, 128, 64]
# ckv: [pages, page_size, 512]  kpe: [pages, page_size, 64]   o: [tokens, 128, 512]
blocks.caption: Keyword arguments as in the test at commit e2d163f; the wrapper source deprecates the older flat plan(qo_indptr, kv_indptr, ...) form with a DeprecationWarning. The LSE comes back in base 2, so it merges with other FlashInfer states.

blocks.md: A classic bug: setting `sm_scale` to $1/\sqrt{576}$ because the kernel's dot products are 576 wide. Absorption only regroups the original product $q^C \cdot k^C + q^R \cdot k^R$, whose head dimension was $128 + 64 = 192$, so the scale stays $1/\sqrt{192}$. FlashInfer's own test comments it as the head dimension before matrix absorption.

Everything else from this course carries over. The plan runs once per step and serves all layers, the states can be split and merged with lesson 3's operator, and the wrapper accepts `use_cuda_graph=True` with caller-owned index buffers. The `backend` argument chooses among several MLA implementations (FA2 and FA3 templates among them); `"auto"` picks by architecture, as in lesson 6.

blocks.question: An MLA decode step (128 heads, all on one H100) serves 2 query tokens per request, as with speculative decoding. Using the lesson's model, which statement is right?
options: Intensity is about 484 FLOPs per byte, above the ridge of 295, so attention is now compute-bound
Intensity stays near 1, because decode attention is always memory-bound
Intensity doubles to about 8, as for GQA with two query tokens
Intensity cannot change, because the KV cache is the same size
blocks.explain: Each cached 576-element row is used by $h_q s_q = 256$ query rows, so intensity is $1.89 \cdot 256 \approx 484$. That is above the H100 ridge, so math, not KV reads, limits the kernel. GQA with $g = 4$ and 2 tokens would reach only 8. The cache size is the same, but it is reused by more rows.

blocks.question: Why does MLA decode reach so much higher intensity than Llama 3 8B's GQA decode?
options: MLA stores the cache in FP8
All 128 query heads share one cached row, so each byte read serves 128 rows instead of 4
MLA decode skips the softmax
The 576-wide rows fit in L2 cache
blocks.explain: Intensity counts how many query rows use each loaded byte. GQA with 8 KV heads shares each KV row among $g = 4$ query heads; absorbed MLA is MQA-shaped, so all 128 heads share one row. Precision is BF16 in this count, the softmax is still computed, and a long cache does not fit in L2.

blocks.md: Absorbed MLA is multi-query attention over a 576-wide shared row: 1,152 bytes per token per layer and 128 query rows per byte. FlashInfer serves it with the same page table, plan/run and merge machinery, through BatchMLAPagedAttentionWrapper with separate ckv and kpe pages.

lessons.title: Beyond attention: sorting-free top-k and top-p sampling

blocks.md: After the last layer, every request needs one sampled token. Take a toy vocabulary of 6 tokens with probabilities 0.04, 0.30, 0.12, 0.24, 0.20, 0.10 and top-p 0.8. Recall top-p (the Build a GPT course covers it): keep the smallest set of most likely tokens whose total reaches $p$, renormalize, sample. Sorted, the running total goes 0.30, 0.54, 0.74, 0.86, so tokens 1, 3, 4 and 2 survive with mass 0.86, and token 1 is drawn with probability $0.30/0.86 = 0.349$.

The textbook implementation does exactly that on the GPU: sort the whole row, take a cumulative sum, mask everything past the cut, and scatter the result back to vocabulary order. FlashInfer's sampling blog (March 2025) quotes vLLM's code for it and points out the cost: a full sort of a row as long as the vocabulary, often 128K entries or more, for every request at every step, spread over several kernel launches. Replacing it, the blog reports, cut overall sampling time by more than 50% for three models served by vLLM on one H100.

blocks.code:
# Sort-based top-p, the pattern FlashInfer replaces (abridged from vLLM code quoted in the blog)
logits_sort, idx = logits.sort(dim=-1, descending=False)     # full sort
probs_sum = logits_sort.softmax(dim=-1).cumsum(dim=-1)
mask = probs_sum <= 1 - p.unsqueeze(dim=1)                   # the low tail
mask[:, -1] = False                                          # keep at least one
logits_sort.masked_fill_(mask, -float("inf"))
logits = torch.empty_like(logits_sort).scatter_(-1, idx, logits_sort)  # unsort
blocks.caption: Illustrative, not run. Each line is at least one pass over the vocabulary, and the sort dominates.

blocks.md: Step one needs no sort: **inverse transform sampling**. Draw $u$ uniformly from $[0, 1)$, walk the vocabulary in its natural order adding up probabilities, and return the first token where the running sum passes $u$. On the GPU one thread block handles one row; it sums chunks (for example 1,024 threads x 4 values) with the block reduce and scan primitives of CUB (NVIDIA's library of CUDA parallel building blocks), skips whole chunks whose sum does not reach $u$, and stops early once it has. That samples from the **full** distribution. Filtering is step two.

The trick is a test that needs no sort. Token $j$ belongs to the top-p set exactly when the tokens **more likely than it** hold less than $p$ of the mass: $\sum_{i:\,p_i > p_j} p_i < p$. Token 2 ($p = 0.12$): above it lie 0.30, 0.24 and 0.20, total 0.74, less than 0.8, so it is in. Token 5 ($p = 0.10$): above it lie 0.86, so it is out. One pass computes that sum.

So: sample a token, test it, and if it fails, every token with probability at or below it fails too. Raise a floor called the **pivot** to its probability, and sample again among tokens above the floor only. That is rejection sampling, and the whole loop runs inside one kernel. Top-k uses the same loop with a count instead of a mass: accept $j$ when fewer than $k$ tokens are more likely.

**Dual-pivot rejection sampling** (FlashInfer 0.2.3) bounds the rounds. Keep a range: `low`, known to fail, and `high`, known to pass. Each round samples among tokens above `low` (with $u$ scaled by $q$, the mass above `low`), sets pivot 0 to the drawn token's probability and pivot 1 to the midpoint of pivot 0 and `high`, and tests both in one pass:

1. Pivot 0 passes: accept the token.
2. Pivot 0 fails, pivot 1 passes: the new range is (pivot 0, pivot 1).
3. Both fail: the new range is (pivot 1, `high`).

Each failed round at least halves the range, so the number of rounds is $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ for floating point precision $\epsilon$. The blog initializes `high` to the largest probability; the kernel at commit `e2d163f` starts it at 1. Samples stay exact, but the worst-case bound loosens: the first rounds that pass pivot 1 only pull `high` down from 1 toward the largest probability.

blocks.title: The top-p rejection loop on the toy row (FlashInfer kernel logic)
blocks.code:
low, high, q = 0, 1, 1
while True:
    u = uniform() * q                  # mass above low
    j = inverse_cdf(probs, u, floor=low)  # no sort
    piv0 = probs[j]
    piv1 = (piv0 + high) / 2
    m0 = sum(p for p in probs if p > piv0)
    m1 = sum(p for p in probs if p > piv1)
    if m0 < top_p:
        return j                       # case 1: accept
    if m1 < top_p:
        low, high, q = piv0, piv1, m0  # case 2
    else:
        low, q = piv1, m1              # case 3

scenes.caption: Round 1: no floor yet, $q = 1$. The uniform draw 0.03 lands on token 0 (it is first in vocabulary order and has 0.04).
Pivot 0 is 0.04 and the mass above it is 0.96, not below 0.8: reject. Pivot 1 is 0.52, with nothing above it: that passes, so case 2 shrinks the range to (0.04, 0.52).

Round 2: draw 0.95, scaled by $q = 0.96$ to 0.912. Skipping token 0, the running sum passes 0.912 at token 5 (0.10). Mass above 0.10 is 0.86: reject. Pivot 1 = 0.31 passes, so the range becomes (0.10, 0.31).
Round 3: draw 0.50, scaled to 0.43, lands on token 3 (0.24). Mass above it is 0.30 < 0.8: accept token 3. Three rounds, and no sort anywhere.

blocks.title: The floor rises; tokens at or below it leave the race

scenes.caption: Round 1: all 6 tokens are eligible. The draw picks t0, the least likely, and the test rejects it.
Round 2: floor 0.04 removes t0; we sample among 0.96 of the mass. The draw picks t5 (0.10), which also fails.
Round 3: floor 0.10 removes t5 too. Every remaining token is in the top-p set, so any draw now passes; this one is t3.
The distribution the sampler produces: the top-p set renormalized by 0.86 (0.349, 0.140, 0.279, 0.233), exactly the sort-based answer, as the script below checks.

blocks.code:
from fractions import Fraction as F
p = [F(x, 100) for x in (4, 30, 12, 24, 20, 10)]
TOP_P = F(8, 10)
above = lambda x: sum(v for v in p if v > x)  # mass above x

def draw(u, low):  # inverse CDF over p > low
    acc = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(p):
        if v > low:
            acc += v
            if acc > u: return i

def step(j, low, high):  # one dual-pivot round
    piv0, piv1 = p[j], (p[j] + high) / 2
    if above(piv0) < TOP_P: return None                 # accept j
    if above(piv1) < TOP_P: return piv0, piv1, above(piv0)
    return piv1, high, above(piv1)

low, high, q = F(0), F(1), F(1)
for x in (F(3, 100), F(95, 100), F(50, 100)):
    j = draw(x * q, low)
    nxt = step(j, low, high)
    print(f"low {float(low):.2f} high {float(high):.2f}: token {j}",
          "accepted" if nxt is None else "rejected")
    if nxt is None: break
    low, high, q = nxt

def dist(low=F(0), high=F(1)):  # exact, by enumeration
    out = [F(0)] * len(p)
    for j, v in enumerate(p):
        if v <= low: continue
        nxt = step(j, low, high)
        if nxt is None: out[j] += v / above(low); continue
        sub = dist(nxt[0], nxt[1])
        out = [o + v / above(low) * s for o, s in zip(out, sub)]
    return out

keep, c = [], 0                       # textbook top-p: sort, then cut
for j in sorted(range(6), key=lambda i: -p[i]):
    if c >= TOP_P: break
    keep.append(j); c += p[j]
ref = [p[j] / c if j in keep else 0 for j in range(6)]
print([round(float(x), 4) for x in dist()], dist() == ref)

Real output: token 0 rejected, token 5 rejected, token 3 accepted; then [0.0, 0.3488, 0.1395, 0.2791, 0.2326, 0.0] True. dist() sums over every possible draw sequence, so True means the rejection sampler's output distribution equals the sort-based one exactly.

blocks.md: Why is the output distribution exact, not approximate? The blog proves it for top-k (top-p is the same argument). Let $T$ be the set to keep and $Z$ its mass. Whatever the current floor, it sits below every token of $T$, because the floor only ever rises to probabilities of rejected tokens or to midpoints that failed. A round draws a token of $T$ in proportion to its probability, or draws a rejected token and starts over with fewer outsiders. Rejected draws never change the relative odds among tokens of $T$, so the token finally returned is $j$ with probability $p_j / Z$. The script checks this by enumerating every path.

Why are rounds few? A round fails only when the draw lands outside the set, and the chance of that is the outsiders' share of the mass still above the floor: 0.14 in round 1 of the toy. Enumerating every path of the toy gives 1.144 rounds on average. Real distributions are peaked, so the outside mass is usually small too, and the dual pivot caps the bad cases. Each round is two passes over the row (a sampling pass that stops early and a pass that sums above both pivots), against a sort plus several full passes.

The API lives in `flashinfer.sampling`: `top_p_sampling_from_probs`, `top_k_sampling_from_probs`, `min_p_sampling_from_probs` (min-p keeps tokens whose probability is at least min_p times the largest), and `top_k_top_p_sampling_from_logits` for the common combination, with `filter_apply_order` either `"top_k_first"` (top-k, then top-p within it) or `"joint"` (both tests in every round). `top_p_renorm_probs` and `top_k_renorm_probs` return the filtered, renormalized distribution instead of a sample, for composing filters. `chain_speculative_sampling` verifies draft tokens with a different rejection test (accept a draft token when a uniform draw falls below the target-to-draft probability ratio) (the optional Speculative decoding course, outside this course's prerequisites, covers the method).

blocks.md: Two traps from the blog and docs. Floating-point prefix sums computed in parallel are not guaranteed to be monotonic even for non-negative inputs, so a naive kernel can return an invalid token; FlashInfer handles this explicitly. And a fixed seed does not make a sample independent of batch position: the docs note that the output row index feeds the random stream, so moving a request to another slot changes its draw.

Sampling is one of several non-attention kernel families in the library now. A quick tour of the docs: [normalization](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/norm.html) (RMSNorm, fused add plus RMSNorm), RoPE, appending new K and V into the paged cache, [GEMM](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/gemm.html) in BF16, FP8 and FP4, [fused mixture-of-experts layers](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/fused_moe.html) with several backends, and [communication](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/api/comm.html) such as all-reduce over CUDA IPC buffers. The list changes fast; the docs are the current reference.

blocks.prompt: Set top_p to 1.0 on the toy row. How many rounds does the rejection loop take, and which distribution does it sample from?
blocks.reveal: Always exactly one round, from the full distribution. A token is accepted when the mass strictly above it is below 1.0, and that mass is at most $1 - p_j$, which is below 1 for any token with nonzero probability. So the first draw always passes and the kernel reduces to plain inverse transform sampling.

blocks.question: On the toy row with top-p 0.8, which first-round draws get rejected?
options: Only draws of token 0
Draws of tokens 2 and 5, the two smallest in the kept set
Draws of token 1, since it alone holds less than 0.8
Draws of tokens 0 and 5: the 0.14 of mass outside the top-p set
blocks.explain: A token passes when the mass of more likely tokens is below 0.8. Token 0 has 0.96 above it and token 5 has 0.86, so both fail; token 2 has 0.74 above it and passes. The rejected mass is $0.04 + 0.10 = 0.14$, the chance round 1 fails. Token 1 is the most likely and always passes.

blocks.question: Why can't the sampler skip the rejection loop and just accept the first inverse-transform draw?
options: Because inverse transform sampling needs sorted probabilities
Because the first draw comes from the full distribution, so tokens outside the top-p set would sometimes be returned
Because the first draw is not random until the pivot is set
Because GPUs cannot compute prefix sums in one pass
blocks.explain: Inverse transform sampling over the unsorted row is correct for the full distribution, which includes the tail that top-p must exclude: token 0 would come out 4% of the time. The test plus resampling above a rising floor removes exactly those outcomes while keeping the relative odds of the tokens that remain.

blocks.md: Top-p and top-k need no sort. Sample with an inverse CDF in vocabulary order, test the draw by summing the mass above it, and on failure resample above a rising floor. The result is exactly the filtered distribution, usually in one or two rounds, all inside one kernel.
